wine.name: Vouvray Le Haut-Lieu
wine.sites: Le Haut-Lieu, the domaine's first vineyard, around the house on the plateau above the town of Vouvray: deep clay over limestone, the softest of its three soils, which gives the most supple of its three wines.
wine.making: Picked in several passes, the grapes of each year decide the style: sec, demi-sec or, in a rich autumn, moelleux. The wine is fermented slowly in old oak casks and in tank, with no new wood, and bottled within a year of the harvest to keep its freshness.
wine.glass: Quince, pear and green apple over lime blossom, beeswax and wool, with a chalky edge; taut as a sec, rounder with a touch of honey as a demi-sec, and always driven by high acidity.
wine.ageing: Bright and open young, it may close for a few years in its middle age and then keeps for decades; the sweet years last half a century.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius for the sec and demi-sec, a little cooler for a moelleux; decant a young sec for half an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The vineyard, a lieu-dit of Vouvray, not an appellation of its own.
Dry: the style the year gave this bottling; another year the same vineyard may be demi-sec.
Medium dry, its sugar balanced by the high acidity of Chenin Blanc.
Sweet, made in rich years from late passes, some berries touched by noble rot.

records.table: Le Haut-Lieu is the first vineyard of Domaine Huet, bought in 1928: Vouvray Chenin Blanc from clay over limestone, made dry, medium dry or sweet as the year allows. It tastes of quince, pear and beeswax, and the sweeter years keep for decades.
records.story: Domaine Huet began in 1928, when a Paris café owner whose lungs had been damaged by gas in the First World War came to Vouvray for his health and bought Le Haut-Lieu, a house and vineyard on the plateau above the town. His son Gaston Huet (1910 to 2002) made the wine with him until 1940, when he was taken prisoner; he spent five years in a camp in Germany, where, as the story is told, he organised tastings and talks on wine for his fellow prisoners. He came home to make the 1947, a hot, rich year that is a Loire vintage of history, and served for decades as the town's mayor. The domaine added the walled Clos du Bourg in 1953 and Le Mont in 1957, and from then on bottled each of its three vineyards apart, dry, medium dry or sweet as the year allowed. His son in law, who made the wines for some four decades, turned the vineyards to biodynamic farming around 1990. In 2003 the family sold a majority of the domaine to an American buyer, who kept its ways. Le Haut-Lieu, the first of the three, is the plainest lesson in Chenin: one vineyard, one grape, and the year deciding whether the bottle is dry or sweet.

others.name: Vouvray Le Mont
others.note: Bought in 1957, on stony clay with flint over limestone; the tautest of the three vineyards.

others.name: Vouvray Clos du Bourg
others.note: The walled vineyard bought in 1953, on thin soil over the rock, giving the most concentrated of the three.

others.name: Vouvray Pétillant
others.note: Traditional method sparkling Vouvray, aged long on its lees.

traps: Sec, demi-sec and moelleux are styles the year decides, not tiers of quality or of vineyard.
Huet's Pétillant is traditional method sparkling Vouvray, not a pétillant naturel.
Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and Clos du Bourg are lieux-dits of Vouvray, not separate appellations.

cards.front: Domaine Huet: what are its three vineyards, and which came first?
cards.back: Le Haut-Lieu, bought in 1928, then Clos du Bourg in 1953 and Le Mont in 1957.

cards.front: What decides whether a bottle of Huet's Le Haut-Lieu is sec, demi-sec or moelleux?
cards.back: The year and the picking: the ripeness and the share of noble rot in each harvest set the style.

questions.q: A guest sees Le Haut-Lieu Sec on the list and, beside it, Le Haut-Lieu Moelleux of another year. What do you explain?
opts: One vineyard, its style set each year by the harvest
Two vineyards of the same name in Vouvray
A dry wine and its sweetened second wine
A Vouvray and a Montlouis from facing banks
questions.exp: Huet makes Le Haut-Lieu sec, demi-sec or moelleux as the ripeness and noble rot of each year allow; it is one lieu-dit, and Montlouis faces Vouvray across the river.

questions.q: Gaston Huet spent the Second World War in a prison camp. Which vintage, made after his return, is a Loire vintage of history?
questions.exp: The 1947, a hot and rich year, is the Huet vintage of history; 1928 is the founding, 1957 the purchase of Le Mont and 1989 the first Cuvée Constance.

wine.name: Coulée de Serrant
wine.classification: A named cru within Savennières, its appellation held whole by one estate
wine.sites: A steep amphitheatre of dark schist above the north bank of the Loire near Angers, enclosed by walls, planted by monks in the twelfth century.
wine.making: The biodynamic grapes are picked late in several passes, some berries touched by noble rot. The juice is fermented slowly with its own yeasts in old oak barrels and kept on its lees for many months, with no new wood, before bottling; the wine is made dry.
wine.glass: Bruised quince, camomile and beeswax over dried apricot, honey and wet stone, dry despite its honeyed scent; broad and powerful, with high acidity, a gentle bitterness and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Often awkward in its first years, it opens with air and with age, and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; decant it hours ahead, since air opens it; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The appellation of this one walled vineyard, inside Savennières, held whole by a single estate.
The wider appellation of dry Chenin on schist near Angers, with two named crus inside it.

records.table: Coulée de Serrant is one walled slope of Chenin Blanc above the Loire, planted by monks in 1130 and set apart as an appellation held by a single estate. Farmed biodynamically since the early 1980s, it is dry yet tastes of honey and quince: decant it hours ahead.
records.story: Cistercian monks planted the slope in 1130, on dark schist above the north bank of the Loire near Angers, and the vineyard has kept its walls and its single shape for close to nine centuries. In the twentieth century the writer Curnonsky (1872 to 1956), the prince of French gastronomes, counted its wine among the five great white wines of France. In 1962 the Joly family bought the estate, with the neighbouring vines of the Roche aux Moines. The founder's son took charge in the late 1970s after a career in banking and, having read the lectures on farming that Rudolf Steiner (1861 to 1925) gave in 1924, turned the vineyard to biodynamics in the early 1980s, an early convert in France. He became the method's loudest voice, writing and speaking for it across the world, and the slope became a place of pilgrimage for growers. Because the whole of the appellation is held by one estate, Coulée de Serrant is a rare case in French law: a vineyard that is a named cru, an appellation and a monopole at once. On a list it is the wine to explain Savennières: dry Chenin of great power, with an argument about farming in every bottle.

others.name: Savennières Roche aux Moines Clos de la Bergerie
others.note: From the neighbouring named cru, Roche aux Moines, a separate appellation next door.

others.name: Savennières Les Vieux Clos
others.note: The estate's Savennières, the introduction to its style.

traps: Savennières Coulée de Serrant is an appellation of its own, held whole by one estate, not a lieu-dit printed on a Savennières label.
Savennières is dry Chenin; Coteaux du Layon, across the river, is sweet.
Roche aux Moines is a separate named cru next door, not a part of Coulée de Serrant.

cards.front: Coulée de Serrant: who planted the vineyard, and when?
cards.back: Cistercian monks, in 1130, on the schist above the Loire near Angers.

cards.front: What farming did Coulée de Serrant turn to in the early 1980s, making it a reference across France?
cards.back: Biodynamics, the farming drawn from Rudolf Steiner's lectures of 1924.

questions.q: A guest orders Coulée de Serrant expecting a sweet wine from its honeyed scent. What do you tell them?
opts: It is dry, as Savennières is
It is sweet, like Coteaux du Layon
It is medium dry, like a demi-sec Vouvray
It is a sparkling wine of Anjou
questions.exp: Coulée de Serrant is dry Chenin, its honey coming from ripeness and age, not sugar; sweet Chenin is Coteaux du Layon across the river.

questions.q: Which family bought Coulée de Serrant in 1962 and later made it a pulpit for biodynamics?
questions.exp: The Joly family bought it in 1962 and turned to biodynamics in the early 1980s; the Huets are Vouvray, the Foucaults Saumur-Champigny and the Mellots Sancerre.

wine.name: Pouilly-Fumé Silex
wine.sites: Parcels around Saint-Andelain on silex, the clay with flint stones of the eastern Loire, which gives the wine its name and much of its smoke.
wine.making: Yields are kept low and the grapes picked ripe. The juice is fermented in oak barrels of several sizes, among them long, narrow casks the founder had made to his own design, and the wine rests on its lees for about a year before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Gunflint, struck match and smoke over grapefruit, lemon zest and white peach, with a little acacia; dense and long, with high, ripe acidity and a stony, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first five years, it then opens and keeps for fifteen to twenty, far longer than most Sauvignon Blanc.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass rather than a narrow one.

label.means: The appellation for Sauvignon Blanc around Pouilly-sur-Loire; never Pouilly-Fuissé, the Chardonnay of the Mâconnais.
The flint clay soil the vines grow on, not the name of a vineyard.

records.table: Silex is Didier Dagueneau's Pouilly-Fumé from flint soils at Saint-Andelain: Sauvignon Blanc from low yields, fermented in barrel and long on its lees. It smells of gunflint and grapefruit and ages like a white Burgundy, so decant it.
records.story: Didier Dagueneau (1956 to 2008) came from a family of growers in the Pouilly hills, but before wine he raced motorcycles, and he kept a racer's appetite for risk all his life. In 1982 he set up on his own at Saint-Andelain with a few rows of vines. Pouilly-Fumé was then mostly a quick, light wine made in steel and sold young, and he set out to show what the place could give. He cut yields hard, ploughed, picked ripe, fermented in barrel and left the wine on its lees, and he had long, narrow casks made to his own design. His neighbours called him a rebel, and his wines divided them, but the flint parcels of Saint-Andelain gave Silex, the bottle that made his name, and beside it came Pur Sang and, from ungrafted vines, Astéroïde. He later planted vines in Jurançon, in the far south west, for a sweet wine, Les Jardins de Babylone. In 2008 he died when his light aircraft crashed, and his son, who had worked beside him, took the domaine on and kept its ways. Silex is the bottle that proves Sauvignon Blanc can age: a Loire white to set beside a grand cru Chablis, never a crisp glass for the terrace.

others.name: Pouilly-Fumé Pur Sang
others.note: From limestone and clay parcels, rounder and more open than Silex.

others.name: Pouilly-Fumé Buisson Renard
others.note: From sandy clay, an exuberant wine of ripe fruit.

others.name: Les Jardins de Babylone
others.note: Sweet Jurançon of Petit Manseng from the domaine's vines in the far south west of France.

traps: Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fuissé is Mâconnais Chardonnay.
Silex names the flint soil, not a vineyard.
Pouilly-sur-Loire is a separate appellation on the same ground, made from Chasselas.

cards.front: Didier Dagueneau's Silex: what does the name mean?
cards.back: Flint: the clay with flint stones in which the vines grow at Saint-Andelain, not a vineyard's name.

cards.front: When did Didier Dagueneau found his Pouilly-Fumé domaine, and when did he die?
cards.back: He founded it in 1982 and died in a light aircraft accident in 2008; his son took it on.

questions.q: A guest asks for Pouilly-Fuissé and points to Dagueneau's Silex on the list. What do you explain?
opts: Silex is Pouilly-Fumé, Loire Sauvignon Blanc
Silex is a Sancerre from Chavignol
questions.exp: Silex is Pouilly-Fumé, Sauvignon Blanc on flint at Saint-Andelain; Pouilly-Fuissé is Chardonnay of the Mâconnais, and Pouilly-sur-Loire is Chasselas.

questions.q: Didier Dagueneau founded his domaine in 1982. What set his Pouilly-Fumé apart from most of the appellation then?
opts: Low yields, ripe picking and barrel fermentation
Steel tanks and early bottling for freshness
Grapes bought from across the Centre-Loire
A share of Chardonnay in the blend

wine.name: Saumur-Champigny Le Bourg
wine.sites: A parcel of old vines near the village of Chacé, on clay and limestone over tuffeau, the soft white chalk of Saumur.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand and fermented in vats in the cellars cut into the tuffeau. The wine is then aged for about two years in barrels, Le Bourg in new oak where the estate's other reds go to older wood, and bottled without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Raspberry, black cherry and violet over graphite, tobacco leaf and a little cedar, the green pepper of Cabernet Franc held in check; fine, firm tannin and a long, silky finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it needs ten years and keeps for twenty and more; old vintages take on the silk of mature Burgundy.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The appellation for red wine, mainly Cabernet Franc, from the villages south east of Saumur.
The name of the parcel, a single old vineyard, not a village or a rank.

records.table: Clos Rougeard is the Saumur-Champigny estate of the Foucault family at Chacé, and Le Bourg is its old vine Cabernet Franc, raised in new oak for years. It shows raspberry, graphite and silk, needs a decade, and then ages like Burgundy.
records.story: The Foucault family has worked vines at Chacé, south east of Saumur, since 1664 by its own account, on clay and limestone over the tuffeau whose cellars run beneath the village. Through the twentieth century, when most of Saumur-Champigny was a light red to drink young, the family kept slower ways: hand picking, low yields, long ageing in barrel and bottling without filtration. Two brothers of the family ran the estate for decades and gave its three reds their shape: Le Clos, the estate wine; Les Poyeux, the perfumed parcel on sandier soil; and Le Bourg, the old vines, raised in new oak where the others went to older wood. They sold little and spoke less, and their wines passed from hand to hand among sommeliers and collectors before they ever reached a wine list. One of the brothers died in 2015, and in 2017 the family sold the estate to new owners, a family that had bought Château Montrose in Saint-Estèphe in 2006. Le Bourg is the bottle that proved Loire Cabernet Franc could stand beside Bordeaux and Burgundy in the cellar, and the reference point for every Loire red that has aimed as high since.

others.name: Saumur-Champigny Les Poyeux
others.note: The perfumed parcel, on sandier soil over tuffeau.

others.name: Saumur-Champigny Le Clos
others.note: The estate wine from several parcels, the Clos Rougeard most guests will meet.

others.name: Saumur Blanc Brézé
others.note: Chenin Blanc from the limestone hill of Brézé, fermented in barrel.

traps: Le Bourg and Les Poyeux are separate parcels, not a village and a cru above it.
Saumur-Champigny is a Cabernet Franc appellation, not a Cabernet Sauvignon one.
Brézé is a hill and a commune of Saumur, and its wine is a white Saumur, not a Saumur-Champigny red.

cards.front: Where is Clos Rougeard, and in which appellation?
cards.back: At Chacé, south east of Saumur, in Saumur-Champigny, on clay and limestone over tuffeau.

cards.front: Clos Rougeard's Le Bourg: how is it raised differently from the estate's other reds?
cards.back: In new oak barrels, where Le Clos and Les Poyeux go to older wood.

questions.q: A guest asks what grape makes Clos Rougeard's Le Bourg. Which answer fits?
questions.exp: Saumur-Champigny is a Cabernet Franc appellation, and Le Bourg is Cabernet Franc alone; Pinot Noir is the red grape of Sancerre.

questions.q: Which family farmed Clos Rougeard at Chacé for generations before the estate's sale in 2017?
questions.exp: The Foucaults farmed Clos Rougeard until the sale of 2017; the Jolys are Savennières, the Huets Vouvray and the Dagueneaus Pouilly-Fumé.

wine.name: Sancerre La Moussière
wine.sites: Domaine La Moussière, the family's home vineyard on the slopes just below the town of Sancerre, on the limestone and marl of the appellation's white soils.
wine.making: The biodynamic grapes come from low yields and are picked by hand. The wine is fermented partly in oak barrels and partly in tank and kept on its fine lees for months, which gives it more weight than most Sancerre, before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, white peach and lemon zest over flint, chalk and a little blackcurrant leaf; fuller than most Sancerre, with fresh acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and open within two years of the vintage, it keeps well for five to eight.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with a tulip bowl.

label.means: The appellation of the hills around the town: white from Sauvignon Blanc, red and rosé from Pinot Noir.
The family's home domaine below the town, a vineyard name and not a classified cru.
The name the head of the family has borne, generation after generation.

records.table: La Moussière is Alphonse Mellot's home domaine below the town of Sancerre: Sauvignon Blanc farmed biodynamically and given months on its lees. It has grapefruit, white peach and flint, more body than most Sancerre; serve it cool, not icy.
records.story: The Mellot family dates its winemaking at Sancerre to 1513, by its own account, and its history tells of an ancestor who in 1698 advised the court of Louis XIV (1638 to 1715) on wine. By family custom the head of each generation came to be called Alphonse, so that the name on the label has passed from father to son for well over a century. The heart of the estate is Domaine La Moussière, the vineyard on the slopes just below the town, and its Sauvignon Blanc carries the name. Through the late twentieth century, when most Sancerre was made quickly in steel to be drunk young, the family turned towards lower yields and longer ageing, and the generation that took charge at the turn of this century farmed La Moussière biodynamically and worked part of its white in oak. Beside it the family bottles an old vine white, Cuvée Edmond, a selection named for its nineteenth generation, and Pinot Noir from single parcels, which shows Sancerre as a red appellation too. La Moussière is the family's signature on a list: a Sancerre with weight and length, a counterweight to the steel bright picture of the appellation.

others.name: Sancerre Cuvée Edmond
others.note: Old vine Sauvignon Blanc, fermented and aged in barrel, the estate's fuller white.

others.name: Sancerre Génération XIX
others.note: A selection named for the nineteenth generation of the family.

others.name: Sancerre En Grands Champs
others.note: Single parcel Pinot Noir, a Sancerre rouge made with Burgundian care.

traps: Each head of the family is called Alphonse, so several Alphonse Mellots appear across the vintages.
La Moussière is the domaine's vineyard name, not a classified cru: Sancerre has none.
Sancerre makes red and rosé from Pinot Noir too, so ask which colour a guest means.

cards.front: Alphonse Mellot's La Moussière: what is it?
cards.back: The family's home domaine below the town of Sancerre, and its Sauvignon Blanc of that name.

cards.front: Why do so many generations of this Sancerre family carry the name Alphonse Mellot?
cards.back: By family custom the head of each generation has been called Alphonse.

questions.q: A guest likes Alphonse Mellot's La Moussière and asks for the red of the same appellation. Which grape will it be?
questions.exp: Red Sancerre is Pinot Noir; Cabernet Franc makes the reds of Saumur, Chinon and Bourgueil, and Côt is the Touraine name for Malbec.

questions.q: By its own account, since which century has the Mellot family made wine at Sancerre?
questions.exp: The family dates its winemaking to 1513, in the sixteenth century; an ancestor is said to have advised the court of Louis XIV on wine in 1698.
